title: Heaven, Hell and the New Creation
summary: The final destinies the Bible describes: the reality of hell, the glory of heaven, and God's promise to make all things new.
description: Where is history heading? This course studies what Jesus and the apostles taught about hell, including the debate over eternal punishment and annihilation, the biblical picture of heaven and the new heavens and new earth, the life of the redeemed in eternity, and how these truths should fuel worship, endurance and evangelism today.
objectives: Teach the biblical doctrine of hell and judgment
Present fairly the views of eternal conscious punishment and annihilationism
Describe heaven and the new creation from Scripture
Explain the life and activity of the redeemed in eternity
Apply eternal realities to daily life and evangelism
outcomes: Compare eternal conscious punishment with annihilationism
Describe the new Jerusalem in Revelation 21-22
Explain why the new creation is physical, not only spiritual
Show how eternity motivates holiness and mission

modules.title: The Reality of Hell
modules.intro: Jesus spoke about hell more than anyone else in Scripture. This week we study what He taught.

lessons.title: Jesus' warnings
lessons.body:
Jesus warned of "hell fire" (Matthew 5:22), of being "cast into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched: Where their worm dieth not" (Mark 9:43-44), and of "outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth" (Matthew 8:12).

He said, "fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell" (Matthew 10:28). At the judgment He will say, "Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels" (25:41).

The word often translated hell is *Gehenna*, the valley outside Jerusalem where idolaters once sacrificed children and rubbish later burned. It became a picture of final judgment.

lessons.title: The nature of hell
lessons.body:
Scripture describes hell with several pictures:

- **Fire**: "the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone" (Revelation 21:8).
- **Darkness**: "outer darkness" (Matthew 25:30).
- **Separation**: "punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord" (2 Thessalonians 1:9).
- **Regret and anguish**: "weeping and gnashing of teeth" (Matthew 13:42).

The pictures differ, but together they describe the loss of every good thing that comes from God. Hell is not a place where Satan rules, but where God's justice is carried out on Satan and all who reject Him (Revelation 20:10).

lessons.title: Why would a loving God send people to hell?
lessons.body:
God is love, and God is just. Hell shows how serious sin is against an infinitely holy God. The judge of all the earth will do right (Genesis 18:25).

God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11). He sent His Son so that whoever believes "should not perish" (John 3:16). People go to hell not because God refuses them, but because they refuse Him: "ye will not come to me, that ye might have life" (John 5:40).

C. S. Lewis observed that in the end there are two kinds of people: those who say to God, "Thy will be done", and those to whom God finally says, "Thy will be done."

terms.def: The place of final punishment for the unrepentant, separated from God's blessing.
The Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, Jesus' word for hell.
A picture of hell as exclusion from the light of God's presence.
The final place of judgment in Revelation, the second death.
Paul's description of the punishment of those who reject the gospel (2 Thessalonians 1:9).
Jesus' picture of anguish and regret in hell.

texts.teaches: Fear Him who can destroy both soul and body in hell.
Everlasting fire is prepared for the devil and his angels.
The lost are punished with everlasting destruction from the Lord's presence.
God has no pleasure in the death of the wicked.
You will not come to me that you might have life.

summary: Jesus taught clearly and often about hell.
Hell is described as fire, darkness, separation and anguish.
Hell was prepared for the devil and his angels.
God is both loving and just; people refuse His offer of life.

options: The Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem

questions.q: For whom was everlasting fire prepared?

options: No one but God's justice; Satan is punished there

questions.q: What does Ezekiel 33:11 say about God?
options: He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked

modules.title: Eternal Punishment
modules.intro: Bible-believing Christians agree hell is real but differ on its duration. This week we study the main views fairly.

lessons.title: Eternal conscious punishment
lessons.body:
The historic majority view, held by Baptists, Pentecostals, Holiness churches including Deeper Life, Reformed and Catholic Christians, is that the lost suffer conscious punishment for ever.

Supporting texts:

- "these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal" (Matthew 25:46). The same word 'everlasting' describes both destinies.
- "the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night" (Revelation 14:11).
- The devil, beast and false prophet "shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever" (20:10).
- "their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched" (Mark 9:48).

lessons.title: Annihilationism
lessons.body:
A minority of evangelicals, such as John Stott (who held it tentatively), hold **annihilationism** or **conditional immortality**: the lost are punished for a time according to their sins and then cease to exist. The punishment is eternal in its result, not its experience.

They point to words such as "destroy" (Matthew 10:28), "perish" (John 3:16) and "everlasting destruction" (2 Thessalonians 1:9); to the teaching that only God has immortality (1 Timothy 6:16); and to the image of chaff burned up (Matthew 3:12).

The majority reply that 'destruction' means ruin, not non-existence, and that Matthew 25:46 places eternal punishment parallel to eternal life.

lessons.title: Views outside orthodoxy
lessons.body:
Some views fall outside biblical teaching:

- **Universalism**: everyone will eventually be saved. This contradicts Jesus' warnings and the call to repent (Matthew 7:13-14).
- **Second chance after death**: Hebrews 9:27 says judgment, not another opportunity, follows death.
- **Purgatory as a path out of hell**: Catholic purgatory is for the saved, not the lost; Scripture knows no escape from final judgment (Luke 16:26).

All faithful positions agree that hell is real, terrible and to be avoided, that God's judgment is just, and that the gospel is urgent. Jesus said the way to destruction is broad, and "many there be which go in thereat" (Matthew 7:13).

terms.def: The view that the lost suffer conscious punishment for ever.
The view that the lost are finally destroyed and cease to exist.
The view that immortality is God's gift only to the saved.
The unbiblical view that all people will finally be saved.
Jesus' phrase for the destiny of the wicked (Matthew 25:46).
Jesus' picture of the easy path leading to destruction (Matthew 7:13).

texts.teaches: The wicked go into everlasting punishment and the righteous into life eternal.
The smoke of their torment ascends for ever and ever.
Their worm dies not and the fire is not quenched.
Broad is the way that leads to destruction.
God only has immortality.

summary: Most Christians hold eternal conscious punishment.
A minority of evangelicals hold annihilationism.
Universalism and second-chance views are unbiblical.
All faithful views agree hell is real and the gospel urgent.

questions.q: Which text places everlasting punishment parallel to eternal life?

options: The lost finally cease to exist

questions.q: Which view is outside biblical teaching?
Which evangelical leader tentatively held annihilationism?

modules.title: Heaven and the New Creation
modules.intro: God's plan ends not with souls floating in the sky but with a renewed creation. This week we study heaven and the new earth.

lessons.title: New heavens and a new earth
lessons.body:
"And I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away" (Revelation 21:1). Isaiah foresaw it: "behold, I create new heavens and a new earth" (Isaiah 65:17).

Creation itself will be redeemed: "the creature itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God" (Romans 8:21). "We, according to his promise, look for new heavens and a new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness" (2 Peter 3:13).

The final hope is not escape from the physical world but resurrection bodies in a renewed physical world, with God dwelling among His people.

lessons.title: The holy city
lessons.body:
John saw "the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride" (Revelation 21:2). The city has gates of pearl, streets of gold and walls of precious stones (21:18-21).

Its greatest glory is God's presence: "Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them" (21:3). "The city had no need of the sun... for the glory of God did lighten it, and the Lamb is the light thereof" (21:23).

The river of the water of life and the tree of life are there (22:1-2): Eden restored and surpassed. People from every nation bring their glory into it (21:24-26).

lessons.title: No more tears
lessons.body:
"And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away" (Revelation 21:4).

What will be absent: sin, the curse (22:3), death, sickness, night, fear and everything that defiles (21:27).

What will be present: God's face (22:4), perfect fellowship, joy "for evermore" (Psalm 16:11), and the company of the redeemed. "Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard... the things which God hath prepared for them that love him" (1 Corinthians 2:9).

terms.def: God's dwelling place, and the eternal home of His people with Him.
The renewed heavens and earth God will make, free from sin and curse.
The holy city coming down from God, where God dwells with His people.
The tree of Eden, restored in the new creation (Revelation 22:2).
Seeing God face to face, the highest joy of the redeemed (Revelation 22:4).
Creation's slavery to decay, from which it will be freed (Romans 8:21).

texts.teaches: John saw a new heaven and a new earth.
Creation will be delivered from the bondage of corruption.
The tabernacle of God is with men, and He will dwell with them.
God shall wipe away all tears; there shall be no more death.
They shall see His face.

summary: God will create new heavens and a new earth.
Creation will be freed from decay; our hope is physical and glorious.
The new Jerusalem's greatest glory is God dwelling with His people.
There will be no tears, death, pain or curse.

questions.q: What will God make, according to Revelation 21:1?
options: A new heaven and a new earth

questions.q: What is the greatest glory of the new Jerusalem?
What will creation be freed from?
What will the redeemed see, according to Revelation 22:4?

modules.title: Living for Eternity
modules.intro: What will we do for ever? And how should eternity shape life now? This week we study the life of the redeemed and its implications today.

lessons.title: What will we do in eternity?
lessons.body:
Heaven is not endless boredom. Scripture describes:

- **Worship**: "Worthy is the Lamb" (Revelation 5:12), with joy, not duty.
- **Service**: "his servants shall serve him" (22:3).
- **Reigning**: "they shall reign for ever and ever" (22:5); faithful servants are given authority (Luke 19:17).
- **Fellowship**: with God and all the redeemed, including Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Matthew 8:11).
- **Rest**: "There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God" (Hebrews 4:9).
- **Learning**: the ages to come will show "the exceeding riches of his grace" (Ephesians 2:7).

lessons.title: Eternity and today
lessons.body:
Eternal realities shape present living:

- **Perspective in suffering**: "our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory" (2 Corinthians 4:17).
- **Priorities**: "Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven" (Matthew 6:20).
- **Citizenship**: "our conversation [citizenship] is in heaven" (Philippians 3:20). We are pilgrims (Hebrews 11:13-16).
- **Hope in death**: "to depart, and to be with Christ... is far better" (Philippians 1:23).

This is not escapism. Hope of the new creation moves believers to work for good now, knowing "your labour is not in vain in the Lord" (1 Corinthians 15:58).

lessons.title: The urgency of the gospel
lessons.body:
If heaven and hell are real, the gospel is the most urgent message in the world. Paul said, "Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men" (2 Corinthians 5:11). He had "great heaviness and continual sorrow" for his unsaved people (Romans 9:2).

The rich man in Hades begged for someone to warn his brothers (Luke 16:27-28). We have the message they need.

The invitation stands open: "And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely" (Revelation 22:17).

terms.def: The final, unending condition of the redeemed and the lost after the judgment.
Eternal rewards gained by living for God's purposes.
Believers' true belonging to God's kingdom (Philippians 3:20).
Believers as travellers on earth heading for their true home.
The glory that far outweighs present suffering (2 Corinthians 4:17).
The fear of God's judgment that moves believers to persuade others (2 Corinthians 5:11).

Lay up treasures in heaven.

Whoever will, let him take the water of life freely.

summary: In eternity the redeemed will worship, serve, reign, rest and learn.
Eternity gives perspective in suffering and right priorities.
Hope of the new creation inspires faithful work now.
Heaven and hell make the gospel urgent.

questions.q: What did the rich man in Hades want for his brothers?

short.q: Summarise what Jesus taught about hell.
short.model: Jesus warned of unquenchable fire (Gehenna), outer darkness with weeping and gnashing of teeth, and everlasting fire prepared for the devil.

short.q: How can a loving God send people to hell?
short.model: God is both loving and just; He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked and sent His Son, but those who refuse Him face just judgment.

short.q: Compare eternal conscious punishment and annihilationism.
short.model: Eternal conscious punishment holds that the lost suffer for ever (Matthew 25:46); annihilationism holds that they are punished and then cease to exist.

short.q: Why is the Christian hope physical and not only spiritual?
short.model: God will raise our bodies and renew creation itself (Romans 8:21), making a new heaven and a new earth.

short.q: What will be absent and present in the new creation?
short.model: No death, tears, pain, sin or curse; and God's presence, His face and perfect fellowship.

short.q: How should eternity shape our lives now?
short.model: It gives perspective in suffering, sets our priorities on heavenly treasure, and makes us urgent in sharing the gospel.

assignments.title: Preaching hell faithfully
assignments.prompt: Many preachers avoid hell; others use it to frighten people. Using the course passages, explain how to teach about hell faithfully, with both seriousness and the love of God. Include a short outline of a sermon on Matthew 25:31-46 or Luke 16:19-31.

assignments.title: The new creation
assignments.prompt: Describe the new heavens and new earth from Revelation 21-22, Isaiah 65 and Romans 8. Then explain how this hope should shape a Christian's attitude to work, suffering and the environment today.
